content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 74 of the Constitution of India is titled “Council of Ministers to aid and advise President”. It forms an integral component of The Union (Articles 52–151), located within the “Union Executive” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice: Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

(2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 74 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. Key aspect: The 42nd made advice binding; the 44th added the reconsideration proviso. The President has almost no personal discretion except in hung-House situations.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice: Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
2. (2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 74 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 74 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 74.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 74 (Council of Ministers to aid and advise President)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 74 (Council of Ministers to aid and advise President) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 74 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “Union Executive” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice: Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
2. (2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 74:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 74 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 74 of the Constitution of India, titled “Council of Ministers to aid and advise President”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 74 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice: Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
(a) Limb 2: (2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 74 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 74 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 74:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 74;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 74 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 74?
Rule: Under Article 74, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 74 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 74 establishes the parliamentary cabinet executive at the Union level. It provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice. It incorporates a proviso permitting the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice once, after which the President must act in accordance with the reconsidered advice.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: India adheres to the parliamentary form of executive governance where the President is the formal constitutional head (de jure), while real executive power resides in the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister (de facto) who are collectively responsible to the House of the People (Article 75(3)).
statutoryFramework: Part V: The Union, Chapter I: The Executive
Article 74 of the Constitution of India
Clause (1): Mandatory Council of Ministers with Prime Minister; binding nature of advice
Clause (1) Proviso: Power of President to return advice once for reconsideration (44th Amendment)
Clause (2): Judicial bar on inquiring into what advice was tendered
Corresponds to Article 163 for State Governors (with discretionary difference)
essentialIngredients: Mandatory Institutional Existence: 'There shall be a Council of Ministers' — the President can never function without a Council of Ministers, even after dissolution of the Lok Sabha (U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi).
Binding Advice: The word 'shall' in Clause (1) makes the advice of the Council of Ministers legally binding on the President.

The One-Time Reconsideration Proviso: The President may require the Cabinet to reconsider its advice once; if the Cabinet resubmits the same advice (with or without changes), the President 'shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration'.
Judicial Secrecy Bar (Clause 2): 'The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court'.

S.R. Bommai Exception: Clause (2) shields the actual advice tendered by Ministers, but does NOT bar courts from examining the **material, reasons, and objective documents** upon which that advice was based.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 74 is the structural bedrock of the parliamentary system in India.

### 1. The Pre-1976 Constitutional Position
Originally, Article 74 stated that there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. In *Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)* and *Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)*, a 7-judge Constitution Bench settled that India adopted the British cabinet system: the President is a constitutional head and must act on ministerial advice in all functions, except in marginal, extraordinary situations (e.g., appointment of PM when no party has a majority, or dismissing a government that has lost confidence).

### 2. The 42nd and 44th Constitutional Amendments
- **42nd Amendment Act, 1976:** Enacted during the Emergency, it amended Article 74(1) to make advice explicitly binding: the President *'shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice'*, eliminating any perceived ambiguity.
- **44th Amendment Act, 1978:** Reconciled cabinet supremacy with presidential dignity by inserting the **Proviso**: empowering the President to return advice for reconsideration once. If the Cabinet reiterates the advice, the President has no choice but to sign.

### 3. Continuous Existence: U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971)
When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, does the Prime Minister and Cabinet cease to exist? In *U.N.R. Rao*, the Supreme Court held that the President cannot exercise executive power without a Council of Ministers. Dissolution of the House does not dissolve the Cabinet; an interim or caretaker government must continue until the new House is constituted.

### 4. Article 74(2) and the S.R. Bommai Landmark (1994)
Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into what advice was tendered. In *S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)*, a 9-judge bench ruled that this bar applies strictly to the actual communications between Ministers and the President. It does NOT bar the Court from calling for the **factual record, reports, and materials** on which the advice was formulated. Judicial review examines the objective material to determine if it is relevant, rational, and free from mala fides.
examples: President Returning Cabinet Recommendation: The Union Cabinet advises the President to promulgate an ordinance regulating agricultural markets. The President, noticing constitutional ambiguities, exercises power under the Proviso to Article 74(1) and returns the file for reconsideration. The Cabinet re-submits the identical proposal without changes. The President is constitutionally bound to sign and promulgate the ordinance.

Disclosure of Documents under Article 74(2): In a challenge to a Presidential Proclamation dissolving a State Assembly under Article 356, the Union Government refuses to produce the Governor's report and intelligence dossiers, citing Article 74(2). Applying S.R. Bommai, the Supreme Court overrules the objection, holding that the underlying material is not privileged under Article 74(2).
distinctions: Article 74 (President) vs Article 163 (Governor): Article 74 does not confer any express constitutional discretion on the President; Article 163 explicitly provides that the Governor acts on ministerial advice 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'.

Actual Advice vs Underlying Material: The actual advice tendered by Ministers is non-justiciable under Article 74(2); the underlying factual material, reports, and evidence upon which advice is founded are fully discoverable and subject to judicial review (S.R. Bommai).
problemApplication: Issue: Parliament passes a controversial Bill. The Union Cabinet advises the President to grant assent under Article 111. The President personally disagrees with the policy of the Bill and refuses to sign it for over a year. Is the President's inaction constitutionally permissible?

Rule: Under Article 74(1), the President must act in accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. Under the Proviso, the President can only return the advice once for reconsideration; persistent refusal to act violates constitutional duty.

Application: While the President can return a Bill once (unless it is a Money Bill), once advice is reiterated or where assent is mandated by cabinet advice, the President has no personal pocket veto against the Cabinet.
Counterargument: The President asserts personal constitutional conscience and inherent discretionary power under Article 60 oath to preserve the Constitution.

Conclusion: In a parliamentary democracy, the President is a constitutional head bound by Article 74; prolonged refusal to act on binding ministerial advice violates the constitutional mandate (Shamsher Singh).

keyTakeaways: President acts on the binding aid and advice of the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister.
President can return advice once for reconsideration (44th Amendment Proviso); must accept resubmitted advice.
President cannot function for a single moment without a Council of Ministers (U.N.R. Rao).
Article 74(2) protects the advice tendered, but does not shield the underlying material from judicial review (S.R. Bommai).
